**Answer: $\dfrac{1-p_0}{1-m}$**

**Approach.** Because $X$ has a stretched-exponential tail with $b<1$, the event $\{M>x\}$ is driven by a single large displacement. Two large jumps are of lower order, and so are paths that reach near $x$ through many moderate steps. So $\mathbb{P}(M>x)$ is asymptotically the expected number of "first crossers": particles whose displacement carries them above $x$ while their parent's position is still at most $x$.

**Convention.** I read the model as one displacement $X_v$ per particle $v$, shared by all of $v$'s children, with the offspring number independent of $X_v$. A particle with no children (probability $p_0$) produces no particle alive at any later time, so it contributes nothing to $M$. This convention is what makes $p_0$ enter the answer.

**Count.** Let $Z_n$ be the generation-$n$ size, so $\mathbb{E}Z_n = m^n$. A generation-$n$ particle with at least one child (probability $1-p_0$, independent of its displacement) produces a first crosser when its displacement exceeds $x$ minus its parent's position. That parent position is $O(1)$ with high probability, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(M>x)\sim \sum_{n\ge 0} \mathbb{E}\big[Z_n\big]\,(1-p_0)\,\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\frac{1-p_0}{1-m}\,\mathbb{P}(X>x).
$$

The root (generation 0) is included, since its displacement produces the first generation. Multiplying by $e^{\lambda x^b}/(\ell(x)x^a)$ gives the stated limit.

**Check.** As $p_0\to1$ (so $m\to0$), the limit tends to $1-p_0$, which is the probability that the root has any children. In that case $M$ is exactly the root's single displacement, so $\mathbb{P}(M>x)\approx(1-p_0)\mathbb{P}(X>x)$, as expected.

This relies on the shared-displacement convention. If each child carried its own independent displacement, the constant would instead be $m/(1-m)$, which does not involve $p_0$.

ANSWER: $\dfrac{1-p_0}{1-m}$
